entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12069"/><div sID="gen21820" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12069"/>7. The Persian king was regarded as representative of the chief god, Ormuzd; the seven princes near him represented the seven Amshaspands before the throne of Ormuzd; hence Mordecai (<reference osisRef="Esth.3.4">Es 3:4</reference>) refused such homage to Haman, the king's prime minister, as inconsistent with what is due to God alone. A weak despot, like Darius, much under the control of his princes, might easily be persuaded that such a decree would test the obedience of the Chaldeans just conquered, and tame their proud spirits. So absolute is the king in the East, that he is regarded not merely as the ruler, but the owner, of the people.<div eID="gen21820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21821" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">All ... governors ... counsellors, &c.--</hi>Several functionaries are here specified, not mentioned in <reference osisRef="Dan.6.4">Da 6:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.6">6</reference>. They evidently exaggerated the case of the weak king, as if their request was that of all the officers in the empire.<div eID="gen21821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">den of lions--</hi>an underground cave or pit, covered with a stone. It is an undesigned proof of genuineness, that the "fiery furnace" is not made the means of punishment here, as in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.20">Da 3:20</reference>; for the Persians were fire-worshippers, which the Babylonians were not. <div eID="gen21822" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12071"/><div sID="gen21826" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12071"/>9. Such a despotic decree is quite explicable by remembering that the king, as the incarnation of Ormuzd, might demand such an act of religious obedience as a test of loyalty. Persecuting laws are always made on false pretenses. Instead of bitter complaints against men, Daniel prays to God. Though having vast business as a ruler of the empire, he finds time to pray thrice a day. Daniel's three companions (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.12">Da 3:12</reference>), are not alluded to here, nor any other Jew who conscientiously may have disregarded the edict, as the conspirators aimed at Daniel alone (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.5">Da 6:5</reference>). <div eID="gen21826" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12077"/><div sID="gen21841" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12077"/><hi type="bold">16. Thy God ... will deliver thee--</hi>The heathen believed in the interposition of the gods at times in favor of their worshippers. Darius recognized Daniel's God as a god, but not the only true God. He had heard of the deliverance of the three youths in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.26">Da 3:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.27">27</reference> and hence augurs Daniel's deliverance. I am not my own master, and cannot deliver thee, however much I wish it. "Thy God will." Kings are the slaves of their flatterers. Men admire piety to God in others, however disregarding Him themselves. <div eID="gen21841" type="x-p"/>

So spiritually, God will shut the roaring lion's mouth (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.8">1Pe 5:8</reference>) for His servants.<div eID="gen21851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forasmuch as before him innocency--</hi>not absolutely (in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.7">Da 9:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.18">18</reference> he disclaims such a plea), but relatively to this case. God has attested the justice of my cause in standing up for His worship, by delivering me. Therefore, the "forasmuch" does not justify Rome's doctrine of works meriting salvation.<div eID="gen21852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21853" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before thee--</hi>Obedience to God is in strictest compatibility with loyalty to the king (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.21">Mt 22:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.17">1Pe 2:17</reference>).
